links.note: Two people measuring the same room with their feet disagree for the same reason the five handspans disagreed in 32699 - the unit itself differs between people.
Picking an instrument for a person's height is 32703's first step - a metre scale or measuring tape rather than a 15-cm scale. (The item's options are not stored.)
A pipe that a straight ruler cannot follow needs the flexible tape 32703 introduces for girths and curved lengths.
The minute hand is circular AND periodic, and it is 32710 that establishes periodicity - that circular and oscillatory motion both repeat after a fixed interval. 32709 defines circular motion only.

The exercise that sends the reader to find every scale at home and school and record the smallest value each can measure - 32711. 32702 states that 1 mm is the smallest on a 15-cm scale, but the survey is the exercise's.
Each centimetre divided into 10 millimetres - 32702, read off the 15-cm scale.
Measuring a friend's height and writing it three ways is 32712's exercise; 32702 supplies the conversions it needs.
Girth of a tree and chest size are 32703's own examples of measurements a straight scale cannot make.
Handspan readings differing because handspans differ is exactly what 32699's five friends established by laying their hands side by side; 32700 then turns it into the case for a standard unit.
The option set turns on standard units against traditional body-based ones, which is 32701's argument for SI.
The surviving fragment is a plucked string, which moves to and fro about a fixed position - oscillatory, and periodic, both in 32710. Stem is truncated: the numbered statements are missing.
A length-unit conversion, which is 32702's content; the inch belongs to one of the other systems 32701 mentions and is not itself in the concept text.
A flexible tape for a tree's girth - 32703.
The windowless vehicle at constant speed is 32708's Think It Over, the limit case of needing an outside reference point to judge motion.
